summary: In traffic-engineered networks it is sometimes desirable to set up an end-to-end path with constraints such as bandwidth across several networks. This best current practice document states the problem of exchanging the traffic engineering information needed for that and describes an architecture, including abstraction of topology, for sharing it between interconnected networks. It is a problem statement and architecture, not a new protocol.

eli5.summary: Planning a road trip across several countries is hard if each country keeps its maps secret. This describes how neighboring road networks can share just enough map information to plan a good route, without revealing everything.

subtitle: How separate traffic-engineered networks can share just enough path information to build end-to-end connections.

tldr.problem: Traffic-engineered (TE) paths with constraints such as bandwidth are hard to set up across several networks, because TE information is usually visible only inside each network (a domain).
tldr.mechanism: Each network applies policy to its own TE information and advertises only abstract links that express the potential to connect. These links form an abstraction layer network on which end-to-end paths can be computed.
tldr.outcome: This is a problem statement and architecture, not a new protocol. It is a Best Current Practice that reuses existing protocols such as BGP-LS, OSPF, IS-IS and RSVP-TE, and it accepts that paths will not always be optimal.

today: RFC 7926 is a Best Current Practice and, according to the metadata for this unit, has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the statement of the problem and architecture for exchanging TE information between interconnected networks, and it describes no new protocol.

sections.title: The Problem and Its Scope
sections.content:
Traffic-engineered systems such as MPLS-TE and GMPLS set up paths through a network in a controlled way that reserves resources on specified links. A path is computed from the Traffic Engineering Database (TED), which is built from information spread by an IGP such as OSPF-TE or ISIS-TE. That information is normally available only inside one network.

The RFC calls such a zone of visibility a domain: any collection of network elements within a common sphere of address management or path computational responsibility. IGP areas and Autonomous Systems are examples. To set up a path across several domains, a computing node does not need all the TE data of each domain. It needs a subset that expresses the potential of providing TE connectivity, called TE reachability information.

The scope is deliberately small. The document limits itself to simple TE constraints (TE metrics, hop count, bandwidth, delay, shared risk) because additional constraints would complicate aggregation and the stability of the mechanism. Section 9 adds that the work is meant for some small set of interconnected, related domains. The aim is not to turn the whole Internet into one large TE network, and it does not promise optimal paths.
sections.eli5: Each network knows its own roads very well but not its neighbors'. To drive across several of them, you need to know only which doors connect to which, not every street.

sections.title: Use Cases: Peers, Clients and Servers
sections.content:
The RFC walks through situations where a path must cross domain boundaries.

  • Peer networks: A source in Domain A needs a path to a destination in Domain Z, and there are two points of interconnection. If Domain A picks the one that has no connectivity onward to the destination, the path cannot be established. Crankback can recover, but it does not give rapid setup or guaranteed optimality, and RSVP signaling creates state that is then removed.
  • Client-server networks: A server network provides connectivity for a client network, which is sometimes called an overlay. Either the client domains are joined by a lower-layer network, or the client is a set of Virtual Private Network (VPN) sites with its own address space connected over a provider core.
  • Dual-homing: A client domain attached to more than one server domain, or attached twice to one, adds further choices.

A client can ask for connectivity by management action or dynamically. Requests range from basic provisioning (end points and capacity), through optimization and constraints, to fate diversity, fate sharing, concurrent provisioning and service resilience. The server network may also answer what-if requests of the form: if I were to ask for this service, could you provide it?
sections.eli5: Sometimes two towns need a road through a third town, or a company needs a private tunnel through a big carrier's network. There are many ways to wire this up, and picking the wrong door can leave you stuck.

sections.title: What a Solution Must Handle
sections.content:
The problem is stated simply: a mechanism is required that lets path computation in one domain make informed choices about the TE capabilities and exit points of other domains. The RFC stresses that this is about information collection and presentation, not signaling. Existing signaling for TE LSPs is likely to be adequate, with possible minor extensions.

Five issues shape any solution:

  • Policy and filters: the operator sharing information, and the one receiving it, must both be able to control what is shared and how it is weighted.
  • Confidentiality: internal topology and loading can be commercially sensitive, so a domain must be able to share only what the computing domain needs. The less is shared, the more likely a less optimal path or more crankback.
  • Information overload: sharing everything would create one single flat network domain.
  • Information churn: as LSPs come and go, available resources change and must be re-advertised. Routers can apply a threshold so small changes are sent only at an update interval.
  • Aggregation: the virtual node model (a domain shown as one node) and the virtual link model (a domain shown as edge-to-edge links) both remove information, which can cause inaccurate results and failed path computation.
sections.eli5: A good plan has to let each network keep some secrets, avoid drowning everyone in maps, and cope with maps that keep changing.

sections.title: Abstraction, Not Aggregation
sections.content:
Aggregation synthesizes new data from available information. The RFC instead uses abstraction: applying policy to the TE information within a domain to produce selective information that represents the potential ability to connect across the domain. It can be viewed as policy-based aggregation.

Abstraction does not offer every connectivity option. It also has a dynamic element but is not intended to keep pace with changes in TE attribute availability, so there is no guarantee that an abstraction is current or feasible, and a computed path might not turn out to be usable. Which connectivity is advertised may depend on commercial relationships, the risk of disclosing confidential information and concerns about how the connectivity is used.

The building block is the abstract link: a measure of the potential to connect a pair of points with certain TE parameters, that is, a path and its characteristics in the server network. It represents the possibility of setting up an LSP, and more than one LSP can be set up over it. The related TE reachability can be described as: you can get from node X to node Y with the following TE attributes.
sections.eli5: Instead of handing over the whole map, a network says: I could build you a road from here to there if you asked. That promise is the abstract link.

sections.title: The Abstraction Layer Network
sections.content:
The architecture adds an intermediary layer between the client and server networks. The abstraction layer network holds the client network edge nodes, the server network edge nodes, the links between client and server, and the abstract links. The client and server networks keep operating as normal, and the abstraction layer is the brokerage between them.

A worked example in the RFC has client nodes C1 to C9 and C0 over server nodes S1 to S9. The server network offers four abstract links: S1-S3, S3-S6, S1-S9 and S7-S9. The client asks for C2 to be connected to C3 and to C0. The abstraction layer then:

  1. asks its PCE to compute paths, giving C2-S1-S3-C3 and C2-S1-S9-C0;
  2. instructs C2 to start signaling;
  3. has C2 signal the LSPs with those explicit routes;
  4. lets the server network support them, if needed by server LSPs used as tunnels or stitching segments;
  5. completes the client-edge-to-client-edge LSPs;
  6. informs the client network, which advertises the new TE links.

The client can then compute an end-to-end path from C1 to C7. The same model covers peer networks, where abstract links across transit networks join the edges, and it allows one server for several clients or one client with several servers. Layers may use separate address spaces, even overlapping ones, but that needs address mapping at the interfaces. The abstraction layer needs a routing protocol of its own, carried over control-plane connectivity that already exists in the server network. The RFC advises caution about fully dynamic abstraction, since stability is more likely to be the desired operational practice.
sections.eli5: Imagine a middle floor in a building where the two neighbors meet. The server network puts offers on the table, the client picks, and the middle floor builds the connection and tells the client when its new road is ready.

sections.title: Building on Existing Protocols
sections.content:
This part is non-normative. The general principle is protocol reuse over inventing new protocols, because that helps network stability, time to deployment and operator training. The RFC accepts that extensions will be needed and says that in extreme cases a new protocol can be better than a messy hack of an existing one.

  • BGP-LS (RFC 7752) announces topology from one network to a northbound consumer, and could advertise abstract links into the abstraction layer or potential connectivity to the client network.
  • OSPF and IS-IS both carry TE information and can run as multiple instances, so either could be the routing protocol of the abstraction layer.
  • RSVP-TE can set up all the TE LSPs the model demands without protocol extensions, with LSP hierarchy or stitching if needed.

In the sketched solution, a GMPLS server network builds a TED, a policy process picks nodes and abstract links, and BGP-LS advertises them. The abstraction layer then computes a path, asks the server layer for tunnels or stitching LSPs if needed, signals the client-edge-to-client-edge LSP and informs the client network. Its control plane must run in an out-of-band control network, because the data links may not yet exist.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a new language, the plan uses the languages routers already speak, with a few small additions.

sections.title: Optical, UNI and VPN Applications
sections.content:
The RFC applies the model to three settings.

  • Optical domains (Section 6): an operator may run a mesh of small domains, each with its own OSPF instance. The area-based and AS-based models fit poorly and raise scaling questions. The third, the ASON model of RFC 6827, is close to this architecture once simplified: zero information is imported to low-level domains, only abstracted links are exported, and no formal routing levels are needed.
  • User-Network Interface (Section 7): the Ethernet UNI service network is equivalent to the abstraction layer network, with client edge nodes as UNI-C and server edge nodes as UNI-N. Modeled this way, there is no need to enhance UNI signaling or add routing exchanges at the UNI.
  • L3VPN across multiple ASes (Section 8): the abstraction layer is made of the CE nodes, CE-PE links, PE nodes and PE-PE tunnels as abstract links, and each VPN can have its own abstraction layer network.

On manageability (Section 10), each layer is managed independently. The special point is that OAM cannot run on links that are only a potential of a link. The abstraction layer may be run by the server operator, by the client operator or by a third party.
sections.eli5: The same middle-floor idea works for optical fiber rings, for company-to-carrier connections and for private networks that cross several carriers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security of signaling and routing is usually handled inside a domain, and domain-based security relies on keeping control-plane messages from entering the domain from outside. This architecture adds the exchange of control-plane information between domains, for example between UNI-C and UNI-N, between BGP-LS speakers, or between peer domains.

The extra attention therefore goes to authentication of peers, assurance that messages have not been tampered with and, to a lesser extent, protecting message content from inspection because it might reveal sensitive information about the networks. The protocols likely to underpin solutions already include such protection and can run over IPsec, TLS and the TCP Authentication Option. The abstraction layer control plane is likely to be out of band, which mirrors GMPLS but not MPLS-TE, and the same security mechanisms can be applied to that out-of-band network.
sections.eli5: When neighbors swap map pieces, they must check they are talking to the real neighbor, that nobody changed the message, and ideally that nobody can peek.
